::: {.week-meta}

Data

App

## By the end of this week you can

- Name the assumptions of regression and say what violating each one affects.
- Read a residuals-against-fitted plot and a normal Q–Q plot.
- Identify an influential case with Cook's distance.
- Explain why normality concerns the residuals, not the raw variables.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. What makes two models nested?
2. What does a VIF tell you? (R2)

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. One can be obtained from the other by fixing some parameters, for example setting paths to zero.
2. How much the variance of a coefficient is inflated because that predictor overlaps with the others: VIF = 1 / (1 − R²) from regressing it on the other predictors.

</details>

## This week in brief

Regression assumes linearity, independent errors, constant error variance and, for exact small-sample inference, normally distributed errors. These assumptions are about the *residuals*, not the raw variables. Later, Amos's maximum-likelihood estimation makes a stronger assumption (multivariate normality), so learning to check residuals now pays off.

## In the session

- Reading residual plots, using the app in quiz mode.
- Outliers, leverage and influence (Cook's distance).
- Bootstrapped confidence intervals in SPSS as one remedy when residuals are not normal.

## After the session

Read the core reading. Start the app in explore mode to see what each problem looks like, then switch to spotting mode.

## Your task this week

1. Run your R2 model with diagnostics. You can paste this syntax into a syntax window rather than finding the menus:

```
REGRESSION
  /STATISTICS COEFF R ANOVA
  /DEPENDENT wellbeing
  /METHOD=ENTER stress support
  /SCATTERPLOT=(*ZRESID, *ZPRED)
  /RESIDUALS HISTOGRAM(ZRESID) NORMPROB(ZRESID)
  /SAVE ZRESID COOK LEVER.
```

2. **Predict first**, then check: will the residual plots show a problem? Describe what you see.
3. Sort the file by the saved Cook's distance (`COO_1`). Look at the most influential case. Refit without it: does anything change that matters?
4. Rerun the model with bootstrapping (Bootstrap button in the Linear Regression dialog) and compare the bootstrap and normal-theory confidence intervals.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. Which assumption violations bias the coefficients, and which mainly affect the standard errors?
2. Why does the normality assumption concern the residuals rather than the variables themselves?
3. What would you report if you found a highly influential case?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. Non-linearity (a wrong model) and omitted variables bias the coefficients. Heteroscedasticity, non-independence and non-normal errors mainly make standard errors, p-values and confidence intervals wrong; the coefficients stay unbiased.
2. The model says Y = a + bX + e and makes its distributional assumption about e. X can have any distribution, and Y need not be normal overall: it is the scatter around the line that should be.
3. That it was found (with its Cook's distance), whether it looked like an error or a genuine but unusual case, and the results with and without it. Remove it only with a substantive reason, and say so.

</details>

## Extra resources

Optional. Each is labelled with when it is worth reading.

- **Short and useful:** @williams2013 corrects two common misconceptions about regression assumptions; @ernst2017 (open access) shows how often assumptions are checked incorrectly.
- **Looking ahead:** [StatWiki: Data screening](https://statwiki.gaskination.com/index.php?title=Data_Prep) covers the same checks you will use before SEM.
